subChunks.title: Capstone: Guild Management Dashboard
subChunks.hookHtml: You've reached the Senior capstone. This challenge synthesises the full Senior toolkit: TypeScript with advanced patterns, TanStack Query for server state, Zustand for client state, React Hook Form with Zod validation, Framer Motion for animations, virtual lists for performance, state machines for complex flows, compound components, accessibility, and error boundaries. Build something production-ready.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
What you're building

A Guild Management Dashboard — a data-rich admin interface for managing an adventurer's guild. Members, quests, rankings, and treasury.

Pages and features

  • /members — Virtualised member list (1000+ members). Filter by rank (Novice/Apprentice/Knight/Master). Search by name. Sort by XP/rank/joined date. Column headers are sortable.
  • /members/:id — Member profile. Fetch with TanStack Query. Edit form (React Hook Form + Zod). Optimistic update on save.
  • /quests — Quest board. Kanban-style columns: Available, In Progress, Completed. Drag to move quests (Framer Motion drag). State machine for quest lifecycle.
  • /treasury — Charts showing XP earned over time, gold distribution, quest completion rates. Heavy components lazy-loaded.

Technical requirements

  1. TypeScript throughout — discriminated unions for quest status, generic List component, typed API responses
  2. TanStack Query for all server data — loading/error/success states, optimistic updates on member edit
  3. Zustand for UI state — selected member, active filters, sidebar collapsed state
  4. React Hook Form + Zod for the member edit form
  5. Virtual list for the member list (TanStack Virtual)
  6. State machine (useReducer or XState) for quest lifecycle transitions
  7. Framer Motion for: quest card drag, page transitions, list item enter/exit
  8. Error boundary around each dashboard section
  9. Accessibility: all interactive elements keyboard-navigable, modals trap focus, errors announced with role=alert
  10. Lazy-loaded treasury page

Suggested architecture

src/
  App.tsx                    — Router + QueryClient + Zustand + ErrorBoundary
  types/
    Member.ts                — Member, Quest, TreasuryData types
  stores/
    uiStore.ts               — Zustand: filters, selected, layout
  hooks/
    useMembers.ts            — TanStack Query hooks
    useQuestMachine.ts       — state machine hook
  pages/
    MembersPage.tsx          — virtual list + filters
    MemberDetailPage.tsx     — profile + edit form
    QuestsPage.tsx           — kanban + drag
    TreasuryPage.tsx         — lazy-loaded charts
  components/
    VirtualMemberList.tsx    — TanStack Virtual
    QuestCard.tsx            — motion.div, draggable
    MemberForm.tsx           — RHF + Zod
    ErrorSection.tsx         — ErrorBoundary wrapper

Acceptance criteria

  1. Member list renders 1000 members with virtualisation — no jank
  2. Filter and search update the visible list without page reload
  3. Member detail loads, edit form validates, save is optimistic
  4. Quest cards can be dragged between columns
  5. Quest state transitions follow the machine rules — invalid transitions are impossible
  6. Treasury page is lazy-loaded (verify in network tab: separate chunk)
  7. All pages have error boundary protection
  8. Keyboard-only navigation works for all interactive elements
  9. TypeScript reports zero errors

Vex: "Senior tier is where you make architectural decisions that compound. The choice to put filters in URL state vs Zustand. Whether quest cards need a state machine or useReducer suffices. Whether to lazy-load the treasury or eager-load it. There are defensible answers on multiple sides — but you must be able to defend your choice. Document your decisions."

storyBeats.text: The guild needs a dashboard. A thousand members. Hundreds of quests. A treasury that grows and shrinks with every completed quest. No scaffolding. A brief. A blank TypeScript file. The full Senior toolkit in your hands.

storyBeats.speaker: Grand Archmage Solomon
storyBeats.text: TypeScript is your contract with the future. TanStack Query is your contract with the server. Zustand is your contract with the UI layer. State machines are your contract with complexity. Accessibility is your contract with every user. These are not tools you pick up and set down — they are the foundation on which production software is built.

storyBeats.speaker: Vex the Interface Weaver
storyBeats.text: Senior ends where Lead begins. You can assemble the pieces. You understand the trade-offs. You can read any React codebase and make it better. The capstone is proof of that. Build something you'd be proud to ship.
You open a blank file. types/Member.ts first. Then the stores. Then the hooks. Then the pages. The architecture takes shape. One decision at a time. One component at a time. Production-ready.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Build the Guild Management Dashboard described in the brief. Minimum testable requirements:

  • <nav data-testid="nav"> visible on all pages
  • <div data-testid="member-list"> on the members page
  • <div data-testid="member-count"> showing the visible member count
  • <input data-testid="member-search"> that filters the list
  • <div data-testid="quest-board"> on the quests page
  • <div data-testid="quest-column"> for each status column (3 total)
  • <form data-testid="member-edit-form"> on the member detail page
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Extend the Guild Dashboard with: (1) Real-time notifications using a Zustand store that receives mock WebSocket events (new quest accepted, member levelled up). Notifications animate in/out with Framer Motion. (2) Advanced filtering with URL state — all filter/sort state persists in the URL so dashboards can be bookmarked and shared. (3) Role-based permissions — a usePermissions() hook from AuthContext controls which actions are available (Guild Master can delete members; Knights cannot). Permissions gate entire UI sections via a HOC.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Walk through the architecture decisions in your Guild Dashboard. For each major piece of state: where does it live, why, and what would break if you moved it? Cover: server data (member list, quest data), UI state (filters, selected member), form state (member edit), quest lifecycle state. Then explain your accessibility strategy — how did you ensure keyboard navigation and screen reader support across all sections?

questions.prompt: The member list has filters (rank, search query). Where should this filter state live?
options: URL search params — filter state is shareable configuration; bookmarking or sharing a filtered view requires it in the URL
Zustand — global state is always more maintainable than URL state
Local useState in the MembersPage component — it doesn't need to be shared
TanStack Query cache — filters are part of the server data layer
questions.answer: URL search params — filter state is shareable configuration; bookmarking or sharing a filtered view requires it in the URL
questions.explanation: Filter state in an admin dashboard is view configuration — users want to bookmark a filtered view, share it with a colleague, or return to it after navigating away. URL params provide this for free. Zustand would lose the state on navigation; useState would lose it on refresh. TanStack Query's queryKey can include the filters, ensuring the right data is fetched for the active filter combination.

questions.prompt: The member edit form needs to show optimistic updates. A member's XP is edited; the UI updates immediately while the save request is in flight. What is the correct approach with TanStack Query?
options: Use onMutate to snapshot the previous cache and apply the optimistic update; use onError to restore the snapshot if the mutation fails; use onSettled to invalidate and refetch
Update the Zustand store immediately and sync to the server asynchronously
Use useState for the optimistic value and only update TanStack Query after success
Set staleTime: Infinity on the query so it never refetches after optimistic update
questions.answer: Use onMutate to snapshot the previous cache and apply the optimistic update; use onError to restore the snapshot if the mutation fails; use onSettled to invalidate and refetch
questions.explanation: TanStack Query's onMutate/onError/onSettled pattern is the canonical optimistic update: (1) snapshot = queryClient.getQueryData(['member', id]); apply update; return { snapshot }. (2) onError receives context.snapshot and restores it. (3) onSettled calls invalidateQueries to sync the server's real state. This gives instant feedback, correct rollback, and eventual consistency.

questions.prompt: The treasury page contains heavy charting components. It's visited by 5% of dashboard users. What is the correct code splitting strategy?
options: Lazy-load the entire TreasuryPage with React.lazy — the charts bundle only downloads when the user navigates to /treasury
Import the treasury components eagerly but render them only conditionally
Move the charts to a separate micro-frontend
SSG the treasury page separately so it loads from a CDN
questions.answer: Lazy-load the entire TreasuryPage with React.lazy — the charts bundle only downloads when the user navigates to /treasury
questions.explanation: Route-level code splitting with React.lazy(() => import('./pages/TreasuryPage')) puts the treasury + chart library in a separate bundle. The 95% of users who never visit /treasury never download it. The 5% who do get a Suspense loading fallback while the chunk downloads (typically < 1s on a good connection). This is the highest-ROI code splitting strategy: separate by route, lazy by demand.
